lessonPlan.title: A White Heron unit
lessonPlan.author: Sarah Orne Jewett
lessonPlan.edition: First published: A White Heron and Other Stories, 1886
lessonPlan.editionNote: Reading text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_White_Heron (revision 15592539), cleaned for Liber et Libri.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 7–11 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in A White Heron.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about A White Heron: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does A White Heron suggest about nature versus progress?
What does A White Heron suggest about loyalty and silence?
What does A White Heron suggest about girlhood?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

wholeBookTest.title: A White Heron: whole-book test

items.prompt: What is the hunter looking for?
What does he offer for information?
How does Sylvia find the nest?
options: She climbs a great pine tree at dawn

items.prompt: In the line “But Sylvia does not speak after all, though the old grandmother fretfully rebukes her, and the young man's kind, appealing eyes are looking straight in her own.”, what does “fretfully” most nearly mean?
options: hard to grasp, catch or put into words

items.prompt: In the line “A little girl was driving home her cow, a plodding, dilatory, provoking creature in her behavior, but a valued companion for all that.”, what does “dilatory” most nearly mean?
options: hard to grasp, catch or put into words

items.prompt: As used in the story (“But Sylvia does not speak after all, though the old grandmother fretfully rebukes her, and the young man's kind, appealing eyes are looking ”), what does “fretfully” mean?
As used in the story (“A little girl was driving home her cow, a plodding, dilatory, provoking creature in her behavior, but a valued companion for all that.”), what does “dilatory” mean?
options: hard to grasp, catch or put into words

items.prompt: As used in the story (“She grieved because the longed-for white heron was elusive, but she did not lead the guest, she only followed, and there was no such thing a”), what does “elusive” mean?
options: joyful and proud especially because of triumph or success
a deep awareness of and sympathy for another's suffering
hard to grasp, catch or put into words

items.prompt: As used in the story (“The good woman suspected that Sylvia loitered occasionally on her own account; there never was such a child for straying about out-of-doors ”), what does “loitered” mean?
As used in the story (“A little girl was driving home her cow, a plodding, dilatory, provoking creature in her behavior, but a valued companion for all that.”), what does “provoking” mean?

answerKey.answer: She climbs a great pine tree at dawn
hard to grasp, catch or put into words

shortAnswer: Explain how nature versus progress develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how loyalty and silence develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how girlhood develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (nature versus progress, loyalty and silence, girlhood) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what A White Heron teaches about nature versus progress. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Sarah Orne Jewett develops nature versus progress in A White Heron. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Sarah Orne Jewett develops nature versus progress across A White Heron. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of A White Heron (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of nature versus progress. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of nature versus progress in A White Heron. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Sarah Orne Jewett's choices in A White Heron (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of nature versus progress, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places A White Heron's treatment of nature versus progress in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on nature versus progress in A White Heron that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on nature versus progress in A White Heron. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about nature versus progress in A White Heron, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on nature versus progress in A White Heron, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
